destination.title: Police Raided the Wrong House and Handcuffed an Innocent Woman

short44: Armed police break down your door.
Wrong house.
You're right — and it's all on camera.
Does the law owe you anything?
A Chicago social worker is changing after a shift
when twelve officers force her door.
She's cuffed before she can cover herself.
They had a real warrant, signed by a judge,
but the address was wrong.
Again and again she says: you have the wrong house.
A body camera recorded all of it.
The city fought two years to bury the video.
A TV station aired it, and the country heard her.
An oversight agency flagged nearly a hundred alleged violations.
But a watchdog's finding is not a court's ruling.
The city paid her two point nine million dollars.
But look what a settlement is.
No court found anyone broke the law.
No officer was declared liable.
The reform in her name was voted down.
The rule guarding your door is still a command —
with almost nothing behind it.
Watch the full story on the channel.
Follow for more.
short52: Twelve officers with rifles just broke down
a door in Chicago.
It's the wrong house
and being right won't save her.
A social worker comes home from her shift.
She's changing out of her work clothes
when her front door caves in.
She's handcuffed before she can cover herself
and she tells them
again and again:
you have the wrong house.
The warrant was real.
The tip behind it was wrong.
The man they wanted lived somewhere else
wearing a court-ordered ankle monitor.
His exact location was on a screen
the entire time.
A body camera recorded everything.
So the city apologized right? No.
It fought in court to keep that video hidden
until a TV station aired it.
Then the city paid her 2.9 million dollars.
Here's the part they don't say:
no court ever ruled a single officer
violated her rights.
The money admitted nothing.
Follow for the cases they don't teach you
full film on the channel.

shorts.angle: The Supreme Court kept the knock-and-announce rule and took away the only punishment for breaking it.
shorts.funnel_question_left_for_longform: What that remaining remedy was actually worth to a woman whose door was the wrong one.
shorts.loop_join: L5 ends with the knock-and-announce rule still standing, and L1 opens by describing that rule, so the loop replays it with the remedy already gone.

lines.text: Before police force their way into your home, they knock and announce. In 2006 the Supreme Court decided what happens when they do not.
source_lines: Before police force their way into a home, they knock, they announce who they are, and they give you a moment to reach the door.

lines.text: Detroit, 1998. Police hold a valid warrant. They announce themselves, then wait three to five seconds before going through an unlocked door. The violation is admitted.
source_lines: Police hold a valid warrant to search the home of a man named Booker Hudson.

and then they wait only three to five seconds before going through an unlocked door. It is not long enough. Everyone in the case agrees it is not long enough; Michigan does not even argue the point. The violation is admitted.

lines.text: The Court answers five to four. The rule is still a command of the Fourth Amendment. Police still have to obey it. What it takes away is the punishment.
source_lines: The knock-and-announce rule, he writes, is still a command of the Fourth Amendment. It still exists. Police still have to obey it. The Court does not say officers can stop knocking.
What the Court takes away is the punishment.

lines.text: The dissent is blunt. Take away the remedy, and you take away the rule. A right with no consequence for breaking it is not really a right.
source_lines: Take away the remedy, he says, and you take away the rule.
A right with no consequence for breaking it, he writes, is not really a right at all.

lines.text: What is left is a civil lawsuit you bring yourself, years after the door is already off its hinges. The knocking rule is still there.
source_lines: The majority's reply is that one remedy still stands — a civil lawsuit.
